verses.en: For every high priest is taken from among the people[NOTE:1] and appointed[NOTE:2] to represent them before God,[NOTE:3] to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.
notes: Grk “from among men,” but since the point in context is shared humanity (rather than shared maleness), the plural Greek term ἀνθρώπων (anthrōpōn) has been translated “people.”
Grk “who is taken from among people is appointed.”
Grk “appointed on behalf of people in reference to things relating to God.”
verses.commentary:
5:1-4 Verses 1-4 describe OT Levitical high priests.

- comes from one specific tribe (Levi)

- stands before God on Israel's behalf

- offers gifts and sacrifices for sin (cf. Heb. 8:3; 9:9)

- deals gently with sinners because he is a sinner (cf. Lev. 16:3,6)

- does not take personal honor, but is honored by God's choice and use

5:1 "on behalf of men" This is the generic use of anthrōpos referring to all human beings (i.e., Heb. 6:16).

5:2

NASB, NRSV
"gently"

This Greek term is used only here in the NT and does not occur at all in the Septuagint. It
is used in Aristeas 256 to refer to the philosophy of moderation (cf. Moulton and Milligan, The
Vocabulary of the Greek Testament, p. 406).

▣ "the ignorant and misguided" In the OT the sins of ignorance and passion were forgivable
through sacrifice (cf. Lev. 4:2,22,27; 5:15-18; 22:14; Num. 15:22-31), but sins of premeditation were not
(cf. Deut. 1:43; 17:12,13; 18:20; Psalm 51).

In Word Pictures in the New Testament, Vol. 5, A. T. Robertson makes the theological
connection between the premeditated sins of the OT for which there was no forgiveness through sacrifice and
the warnings of Heb. 3:12 and 10:26. His statement is "for deliberate apostasy (3:12; 10:26) no pardon is
offered" (p. 368).

Lev. 9:7-17 (initial consecration; Lev. 16:6-19, Day of Atonement; and Heb. 9:7. We learn from Heb. 7:26,27 that
Jesus never had to make an offering for His own sin (see full list of verses at Heb. 4:15), but He does understand our need (cf. Heb. 4:15).

verses.commentary:
5:4 "no one takes the honor to himself" God appointed a certain tribe (Levi) and a certain family
(Aaron's, cf. Exod.28:1; 1 Chr. 23:13) to act as priests (cf. Num. 16:40; 18:7; 1 Sam. 12:9-14; 2 Chr. 16:18). In a

verses.commentary:
5:5 "Christ did not glorify Himself" See John 8:50,54.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (doxa, NT)

▣ "become a high priest" It would be very difficult to convince a group of Jews that Jesus was
High Priest when He did not come from the line of Levi. That is the purpose of this extensive argumentation
(cf. Heb. 4:14-5:10; 6:13-7:28) based on OT quotes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS AS HIGH PRIEST

▣ "but He who said" The author asserts that the Father affirms Jesus' exalted position by
quoting two key royal Psalms, Ps. 2:7 and esp. Ps. 110:4. The Father quoted this same Psalm combined with Isa. 42:1

- at Jesus' baptism (cf. Heb. 3:17)

- at His transfiguration (cf. Matt. 17:5)

Arius (i.e., in the fourth century A.D.) in his theological conflict with
Athanasius over the full Deity of Jesus, used the second part of this quote to assert that Jesus was the
first and highest creation of God (cf. Prov. 8:22-31), but the thrust of the quote is Jesus' sonship
(cf. Heb. 1:2; 3:6; 5:8; 7:28). The original psalm was an annual renewal ceremony for the King of Israel
of Judah.

notes: Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
A quotation from Ps 110:4.
verses.commentary:
5:6 "you are a priest forever

According to the order of Melchizedek" This is a quote from
Ps. 110:4. This Psalm is unique in the fact that it specifically gives the Messiah both a priestly and a
kingly office (i.e., the two olive trees, cf. Zech. 4:3,11-14; and i.e., Joshua as a branch, cf. Zech. 6:13).
We learn from the Dead Sea Scrolls (i.e., Cave 11) that the Essenes were expecting two Messiahs, one royal and one priestly.
Jesus fulfilled both offices. As a matter of fact, He fulfills all three OT anointed offices: prophet, priest
and king (cf. Heb. 1:1-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

▣ "Melchizedek" The full development of this theme is in chapter 7. The imagery is taken from
Gen. 14:17-20, where he is a Canaanite priest/king of Salem (Jebus, Jerusalem).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MELCHIZEDEK

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALEM

verses.en: During his earthly life[NOTE:1] Christ[NOTE:2] offered[NOTE:3] both requests and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his devotion.
notes: Grk “in the days of his flesh.”
Grk “he”; the referent (Christ) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “who…having offered,” continuing the description of Christ from Heb 5:5-6.
verses.commentary:
5:7 "In the days of His flesh" This refers to Jesus, not Melchizedek. It does not mean to imply that
Jesus is not still human. Jesus became Incarnate and remains Incarnate forever.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FLESH (SARX)

▣ "prayers and supplications with loud crying and tears" This may relate to Jesus'

- Gethsemane experience in Matt. 26:37 and Luke 22:44. This is possibly related to the rabbis' three levels of prayer,
showing the intensity of Jesus' emotion in the Garden of Gethsemane.

- His high priestly prayer in John 17 the night of the disciples' Passover meal before Gethsemane.

Number 1 fits this context best.

▣ "to the One able to save Him from death" Was Jesus afraid of death? Death is a natural human
fear and Jesus was fully human (cf. Heb. 2:14). Supremely I think He was afraid of the loss of fellowship with the Father
(cf. Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22). He knew who He was and why He came (cf. Mark 10:45; Matt. 16:21).

All three persons of the Trinity were involved in Jesus' resurrection, not just the Father.

- the Spirit, Rom. 8:11

- Jesus, John 2:19-22; 10:17-18)

- Usually the NT asserts that it was the Father who raised Jesus (cf. Acts 2:24; 3:15; 4:10; 5:30; 10:40; 13:30,33,34,37;
17:31; Rom. 6:4,9; 10:9; 1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14; Gal. 1:1; Eph. 1:20; Col. 2:12; 1 Thess. 1:10).

This phrase may reflect several OT texts that assert that YHWH will save the Messiah

- from physical death (cf. Ps. 33:19; 56:13 or Hosea 13:14)

- will resurrect Him from death (cf. Ps. 16:10; 49:15; 86:13)

▣

NASB
"He was heard because of His piety"

NKJV
"and was heard because of His godly fear"

NRSV
"he was heard because of his reverent submission"

TEV
"Because he was humble and devoted, God heard him"

NJB
"winning a hearing by his reverence"

Peshitta
"and verily he was heard"

This phrase, like Rom. 1:4, was used to support the theological heretical concept of
"adoptionism," which asserts that God rewarded the man Jesus because of His godly, obedient life. The NT
as a whole presents the paradox that Jesus was incarnate Deity and was rewarded for His good service!
Somehow, both are true.

The differences in the English translations come from the ambiguity of the Hebrew term
"fear," especially as it is used of mankind's relationship to God. It seems that it means "reverent awe"
or piety, not "terror of." Its basic meaning is "to hold on to securely" in the sense of doing the known
will of God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

verses.zh: 他虽然为儿子，还是因所受的苦难学了顺从。
verses.en: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through the things he suffered.[NOTE:1]
notes: There is a wordplay in the Greek text between the verbs “learned” (ἔμαθεν, emathen) and “suffered” (ἔπαθεν, epathen).
verses.commentary:
5:8 "Although He was a Son" The word "son" should not be capitalized. It is another in a series of
the comparisons between a family member versus a family servant (ANARTHROUS, cf. Heb. 1:2; 3:6; 5:8; 7:28).

▣ "He learned obedience from the things which He suffered" This whole section has emphasized
both Jesus as a "son" of God (cf. Heb. 4:14) and yet human (cf. "in the days of His flesh" Heb. 5:7).
He was tempted; He prayed; He cried; He suffered; He learned obedience! It is difficult theologically to
hold Jesus' true Deity and true humanity as one truth (one nature). Throughout Church history, heresies
have developed when either side is depreciated (cf. 1 John 4:1-3).

It is hard for believers to realize that they must follow Jesus' example. This was the
problem the believing recipients faced. Would they, like Jesus, follow through to the end, even it if
involved suffering? Suffering is part of the package (cf. Heb. 2:10; Matt. 5:10-12; John 15:18-21; 16:1-2;
17:14; Rom. 8:17; 2 Cor. 4:16-18; 1 Pet. 4:12-19).

How could Jesus be perfected if He was Deity? This must refer to His human development
(cf. Luke 2:40,52). Suffering served a purpose of developing trust as nothing else could do. If it is true
that God's goal for every believer is Christlikeness (i.e., Rom. 8:29; Eph. 4:13), then why do modern
Christians flee the very mechanism that produces maturity?

▣ "learned. . .suffered" These two Greek terms sound very similar.

- emathen ‒ learned (AORIST ACTIVE INDICATIVE SINGULAR)

- epathen ‒ suffered (AORIST ACTIVE INDICATIVE SINGULAR)

Suffering is a necessary teacher!

5:9 "And having been made perfect" This is an AORIST PASSIVE (deponent)
PARTICIPLE. The word "perfect" means "mature" or "fully equipped for the assigned task" (i.e., Eph. 4:12). The
perfection or maturity of both Jesus and His followers is a central concept in Hebrews (cf. Heb. 2:10; 5:9,14;
6:1; 7:11,19,28; 9:9,11; 10:1,14; 11:40; 12:2,23).

been three titles for Jesus mentioned:

- son

- apostle

▣ "the order of Melchizedek" Melchizedek is alluded to because he is the only person
in the OT who is called both priest and king, and who adequately fulfills the theological requirements of this
rabbinical argument. Melchizedek is a rather shadowy figure of Gen. 14:17-20 and Ps. 110:4 who is used to describe
the superiority of Jesus' priesthood over the Aaronic priesthood. See full discussion in chapter 7.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MELCHIZEDEK

verses.zh: 论到麦基洗德，我们有好些话，并且难以解明，因为你们听不进去。
verses.en: On this topic we have much to say,[NOTE:1] and it is difficult to explain, since you have become sluggish[NOTE:2] in hearing.
notes: Grk “concerning which the message for us is great.”
Or “dull.”
verses.commentary:
5:11 "him" This PRONOUN can be either MASCULINE or NEUTER.
I think the NEUTER fits better (cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NIV). Therefore, it would refer to Jesus'
Melchizedekian priesthood. Hebrews 5:11-6:20 is a theological parenthesis. The author will return to
Melchizedek in Hebrews 7.

▣ we" This may be a literary PLURAL, and refers to the one author or a missionary team.

▣ "you have become dull of hearing" This context is unique in Hebrews in that three
PRONOUNS are used:

- "you" (Heb. 5:11,12; 6:9-12)

- "we" and "us" (Heb. 5:11; 6:1-3,9)

- "those" and "they," "them" (Heb. 6:4-8)

See contextual Insights, D. This seems to support the supposed historical reconstruction
that the book of Hebrews was written to a group of believing Jews still content to worship in a synagogue
setting with unbelieving Jews, never fully embracing the consequences of the gospel.

This is a PERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE, which emphasizes a settled state of being.
The term "dull" is used only twice in the NT, here and in Heb. 6:12. The author was having difficulty
explaining, not because of the subject matter, but because of the immaturity of the readers. They had become
hard of hearing and lazy in spiritual matters.

verses.commentary:
5:12 "For though by this time you ought to be teachers" Although these believers had been Christians
for a long period they had not matured. Length of time is not directly related to maturity. It seems they
were continuing to fellowship with unbelieving Jews on the basis of non-controversial Jewish subjects
(cf. Heb. 6:1-2). This was possibly

- to avoid governmental persecution

- to avoid the "great commission" commitment required of Christians

▣

NASB
"elementary principles"

NKJV
"first principles"

NRSV
"the basic elements"

TEV
"the first lessons"

NJB
"the elements of the principles"

Peshitta
"the primary writings"

This term has many possible meanings (i.e., wide semantical field).

- the basic teachings of a subject

- the origin of a subject

- angelic powers (cf. Gal. 4:3,9; Col. 2:8)

- governmental authorities

In this context #1 seems best. The author asserts that these immature believers need the basics
of Christianity taught to them (use # 1), but in Heb. 6:1, definition #2 fits best because 6:1-2 relates
to Jewish teaching, not uniquely Christian teachings, which they are to move beyond. The Greek word here
is stoicheia, while in Heb. 6:1 it is archē.

▣ "oracles of God" This term is used of OT truths in Acts 7:38 and Rom. 3:2.

▣ "milk. . .solid food" These are both God given and both are appropriate at certain times.
However, milk is inappropriate for the mature (cf. 1 Cor. 3:2; 1 Pet. 2:2).

verses.en: For everyone who lives on milk is inexperienced in the message of righteousness because he is an infant.
verses.commentary:
5:13 "word of righteousness" The interpretive question is how does this phrase relate to the "good
and evil" of Heb. 5:14? The NJB translates the first as relating to doctrine, "the doctrine of saving
justice." The TEV translates them as parallel.

- "right and wrong" (Heb. 5:13)

- "good and evil" (Heb. 5:14)

The first phrase deals with a problem of immaturity, while the second deals with a problem
of lack of action/experience.

It is possible that this phrase is in contrast to "the elementary principles" of Heb. 5:12;
6:1. Thereby, it would refer to the gospel as over against Jewish doctrines of Hebrews 6:1-2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

verses.zh: 惟独长大成人的才能吃干粮；他们的心窍习练得通达，就能分辨好歹了。
verses.en: But solid food is for the mature, whose perceptions are trained by practice to discern both good and evil.
verses.commentary:
5:14 "the mature" This term is from the same Greek root translated "perfect" in Heb. 5:9.
Telos means mature, fully equipped for an assigned task (i.e., Eph. 4:12). Jesus' humanity is an example of
faithfulness and growth to maturity (cf. Heb. 5:8-9), just as the readers' lives must be. These believing
Jews had experienced some persecution (cf. Heb. 12:4), but they tended to pull back (cf. "shrink back,"
10:38) into the relative safety of Judaism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: END OR FULL (telos)

▣ "because of practice have their senses trained" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE,
which speaks of repeated action that has become consolidated into a settled state of being-practice makes
perfect! The same VERB is used of God's disciples in Heb. 12:11.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- In Heb. 3:1 two terms are introduced to describe Jesus: "apostle" and "High Priest." The second
one is uniquely developed in Hebrews (cf. Heb. 2:17; 3:1; 4:14-15; 5:5,10; 6:20; 7:26,28; 8:1,3;
9:11; 10:21).

- The author of Hebrews knew that the concept of Jesus (from the tribe of Judah) as High Priest
would be difficult for his Jewish recipients to accept.

- The literary unit, Heb. 5:11-6:20, is a parenthesis in the author's discussion about Melchizedek to warn
both the believing Jews and the unbelieving Jews. Following R. E. Glaze, No Easy Salvation (ISBN 0-914520-06-7),
I believe Hebrews is written to a Jewish synagogue, which included Jews who believed Jesus was the Messiah and Jews
who did not accept this truth.

- In Heb. 5:11-6:20 we have three key PRONOUNS: "we" (5:11); "you"
(5:11-12-three times); and "those"/"they" (6:4-8). These PRONOUNS reflect
three groups.

- "we" and "us," 5:11; 6:1-3, the writer and his/her missionary team

- "you," 5:11-12; 6:9-12, the believing Jews to whom the author is writing

- "those" and "they," 6:4-8, the unbelieving Jews who are co-worshipers and friends of
the recipients of the letter

These three PRONOUNS are a textual key to my interpretation of the difficult chapters of
Hebrews 6 and 10. The issue is to whom are these terrible warnings addressed? I think that there are two sets of
warnings.

- those to unbelieving Jews

- those to believing Jews

- The VERB teleioō ("make perfect") is used repeatedly in Hebrews.

- Heb. 2:10, Jesus made perfect through suffering

- Heb. 5:9, Jesus made perfect and became the source of eternal salvation

- Heb. 7:19, Mosaic Law made nothing perfect

- Heb. 7:28, Jesus made perfect

- Heb. 9:9, Mosaic ritual not able to make worshipers' consciences perfect

- Heb. 10:1, Mosaic ritual unable to make worshipers perfect

- Heb. 10:14, Jesus' offering made believers perfect forever

- Heb. 11:40, OT and NT saints perfected together

- Heb. 12:23, spirits of righteous men made perfect
